catalog_quote: Stress in Nukna is bounded, falling into a bisyllabic stress window at the beginning of the word. Within this window, stress is trochaic (left- headed). (1) hála ['hʌ.la] ‘almost’ ... ámna ['ʌm.na] ‘man’ (2) kaláhu ['ka.lʌ.hu] ‘three’ ... máriya ['mʌ.ɾi.ja] ‘later’ However, Nukna is a variable stress language that is quantity-sensitive. That is, heavy syllables within the stress window may attract stress (in Nukna, a syllable is considered heavy if it is a closed by a consonant). However, a heavy syllable only attracts stress if the first syllable in the stress window contains the vowel [ʌ]. (3) káyam [kʌ.'yam] ‘enemy’ kárang [kʌ.'ɾaŋ] ‘bamboo’ márum [mʌ.'ɾum] ‘owner’ (4) kisum ['ki.sum] ‘coconut shell’ kuhát ['ku.hʌt] ‘frog’ mukam ['mu.kam] ‘cloud’ ... new_statements.quote: Stress in Nukna is bounded, falling into a bisyllabic stress window at the beginning of the word. Within this window, stress is trochaic (left-headed). However, the second syllable in the stress window will attract stress if it is a heavy syllable (CVC) and if the first syllable in the stress window contains the vowel [ʌ]. It is difficult to clearly hear the stress on bisyllabic words that end in a heavy syllable. Stress has not been found to be contrastive. See the Nukna Grammar Sketch (Taylor: 2015) for a more detailed description of stress in Nukna.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog holds a Nukna record (catalog-all-2026-09-12) with an empty rule and there are no existing stress statements, so nothing to contradict; this work supplies the placement rule: initial-window trochaic default with a weight-plus-vowel-quality condition shifting stress to a heavy second syllable, non-contrastive. It is compatible with the blank catalog entry and adds the full rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls in a two-syllable window at the left edge of the word and is trochaic by default, i.e. on the first syllable (táwi [ˈtʌ.wi], sarindet [ˈsa.ɾi.ndɛt], ángárángá [ˈʌ.ŋʌ.ɾʌ.ŋʌ]); it shifts to the second syllable only when that syllable is heavy (closed, CVC) and the first syllable has the vowel [ʌ] (kákáuk [kʌ.ˈkʌuk], kápik [kʌ.ˈpik], háram [hʌ.ˈɾam]). Heavy syllables outside the window never attract stress. Stress is not contrastive (predictable).
new_statements.secondary_stress: The OPD text says nothing explicit about secondary stress; one four-syllable example in its syllable-pattern list carries two stress marks, isikimo [ˈi.si.ˈki.mo] 'small' (p. 5). The fuller source it points to, Taylor 2015 Nukna Grammar Sketch §2.4 (already held by the project under, not in this works list), states that four-syllable words have a second, trochaic, quantity-sensitive bisyllabic window carrying secondary stress ([ˈi.si.ˌki.mo], [ˈtu.tu.ˌwat.nʌ]).
new_statements.exceptions: The text flags that stress is hard to hear on bisyllabic words ending in a heavy syllable. Its own example transcriptions include forms the stated rule does not generate: párumá [pʌ.ˈɾu.mʌ] 'yellow' (second syllable stressed although open), sopsopmá [sop.ˈsop.mʌ] 'slippery' (second syllable stressed although the first vowel is not [ʌ]), hilápmá [ˈhi.ˈlʌp.mʌ] 'morning' (two stress marks); these are given as data, not discussed as exceptions.
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD describes Nukna [ISO 639-3 klt], Uruwa branch of Finisterre-Huon, spoken in Hamelengan, Komutu and Siang villages, Morobe Province (population 930 in the 2000 census); no dialect is singled out. The same author's Taylor 2015 grammar sketch is the source of the rule and covers the same variety.
